dossiers.title: Electrician Simulator
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: The game turns repair work into accessible first-person tasks such as replacing sockets and lamps, drawing wires, inspecting rooms and reassembling workshop appliances.
Jobs arrive as client assignments, supplemented by device repair and garage work; completing them and buying parts form a simple service-business cycle rather than an open-ended electrical sandbox.
The connecting, matching and disassembly minigames are approachable without prior electrical training, but even knowledgeable players rarely encounter realistic circuit calculation or diagnosis.

Qualified or aspiring electricians repeatedly report unrealistic wiring shortcuts and omitted safety, electrical code and circuit details, making it a simplified puzzle rather than dependable job training.
Repetitive actions such as fastening screws, drawing obvious connections and repeating short assignments can feel padded once the limited range of puzzles becomes familiar.
Completing orders earns money to spend on equipment and workspace improvement, but some players find those reward loops too light to make repeated jobs interesting.
Several players find the laid-back process of disassembling devices and restoring working fixtures pleasant, aided by readable object models and an undemanding presentation.
What begins as pleasant hands-on work can slow down through lengthy animations or repeated clicking, especially for players expecting quicker diagnostics or deeper challenges.

The theme gives a playful sense of practicing an occupation, but its deliberately limited educational realism means its strengths are casual tinkering and satisfying completion rather than authentic simulation.

conflicts.statement: Players new to electrical work enjoy simple repair puzzles, while experienced tradespeople often find the omitted wiring practices and technical depth actively misleading or dull.

dossiers.title: Mutazione
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Play centers on Kai's visit to an isolated mutant community, with a day-part schedule of conversations, short errands and changing character interactions.
The richly characterized island residents and their intimate conflicts are a central attraction, gradually blending cozy everyday conversations with grief, secrets and supernatural history.
Exploration and dialogue are simple and story-directed, with seed collecting and musical garden cultivation supplying a calmer secondary activity rather than demanding mechanical challenges.
The deliberate, unhurried structure gives conversations and setting room to breathe, but players seeking regular action or immediately visible goals can find it painfully slow.
Hand-illustrated colorful scenery, distinctive character animations, ambient sound and the garden's gentle musical elements repeatedly draw praise.
Progress often entails walking back through familiar village spaces and revisiting characters at different times of day; some enjoy this routine, while others consider it tedious backtracking.
The mostly fixed dialogue outcomes and lightweight garden puzzles may leave players who want substantial choices or systems-driven gardening unsatisfied.
Some viewers respond warmly to the gentle depiction of acceptance and community, while others find the emotional tone overly sentimental or the protagonist's voice unconvincing.
The story reaches a deliberate ending over several in-game days; the absence of extensive post-story free-roaming can disappoint players hoping to keep visiting their gardens.

conflicts.statement: The muted interactivity and gentle pace are regarded as immersive storytelling by some, but as unrewarding walking and trivial gardening by others.

dossiers.title: She Sees Red - Interactive Movie
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: This full-motion-video crime thriller periodically presents time-limited binary decisions between filmed scenes; interaction is choosing story routes, not controlling a character or solving conventional puzzles.
Each pass takes roughly half an hour, and subsequent choices reveal intersecting perspectives and one of four endings, so multiple viewings are necessary for a fuller understanding.
Players often enjoy energetic direction, convincing production values, violent action staging and a suspenseful soundtrack despite the small-scale filmed setting.
Rewatching branches opens substantially different footage, with scene skipping making later replays shorter, though completing every branch or scene achievement can become repetitive.
The initial mystery deliberately withholds context until alternative paths are watched; some appreciate the recontextualization while others find the plot confusing or full of gaps.
The brevity, limited number of decisions and occasional quick choice timers create friction for players expecting a lengthy film or deeper interactivity.
Players can use the original Russian performances or an English-dubbed version; several viewers consider the English voice lip synchronization less natural than the Russian track.
Opinions about the acting and writing diverge: some find the performances engaging and the story coherent after replay, while others criticize stiff acting or weak plot resolution.
Because the experience involves brief prompted decisions rather than a skill or resource system, mastery is mainly identifying branches and remembering which filmed scenes have been seen.

conflicts.statement: Branching choices and short runtime make it easy to explore different scenes, but the same compact duration and thin interaction disappoint those expecting fuller cinematic or gameplay depth.
